blocks.text: In dovecotes, doves have ארבות arubboth, that is, windows or openings, in which they usually hide and nest. Es. LX, 8. Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves אל ארבותיהם, to their windows? That is, לגו שובכיהון, to their dovecotes, as the Chaldee has it. But when afraid they hide anywhere: in pits, in rocks, in mountains, etc. Hence in Ierem. XLVIII, 28. the Moabites, who for fear of the enemy abandon their cities and hide in caves in the cliffs, are said to be כיונה תקנן בעברי פי פחת, like the dove that (in a similar fear, contrary to its nature) nests in the sides of the mouth of a pit. There the Chaldee has כיונא דשבקא פום שובכה ונחתא ושריא בארעית גובא, like a dove that leaves the opening of the dovecote and goes down to dwell at the bottom of a pit ^{(1)}. And in Cant. II, 14. by the dove that [II, 546] hides בחגוי הסלע בסתר המדרגה, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding place of the cliff, the Hebrews understand the Israelites, whom at the exodus from Egypt Pharaoh pursued on one side, while on the other the desert, full of snakes, hemmed them in. Hence the Chaldee translator: הות מתילא כנישתא דישראל ליונתא דסגירא בחגוי טנרא והיוא מעיק לה מגיו וגצא מעיק לה מברא, The Israelite congregation was like a dove shut up in the clefts of the rock. And the serpent besieges it from within, and the hawk from without. R. Selomo develops this at greater length. So too in Quintus of Smyrna, book 12:
Ἴρηξ σεῦε πέλειαν· ἐπειγομένη δ᾽ ἄρα κείνη Κηραμον ἐς πέτρης κατεδύσατο· — — [Irēx seue peleian; epeigomenē d' ara keinē Kēramon es petrēs katedysato]
A hawk was pursuing a dove; and she, hard pressed, slipped into a hollow of the rock. This is taken from these lines of Homer, Iliad φ᾽ [phi], line 495:
— — — φύγεν, ὥς τε πέλεια, Ἥ ῥάθ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἴρηκος κοίλην εἰσέπτατο πέτρην· [phygen, hōs te peleia, Hē rhath' hyph' irēkos koilēn eiseptato petrēn]
She fled like a dove that, before a hawk, has flown into a hollow rock, into a cave. Yet these lines of the Poet suggest that doves nest in caves even apart from fear:
As a dove suddenly startled from a cave, whose home and sweet nests are in the hollow rock.

So too we read in Diodorus that Semiramis was exposed εἰς τινας ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος [eis tinas erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous, en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos], in certain desert and rocky places, in which, since a great number of doves used to nest there, etc., if indeed doves in the proper sense are meant there. Also in Ezech. VII, 16. those who escaped a great slaughter are said to wander on the mountains כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys. These, that is, for fear of the fowler or the hawk, abandon their natural home and are forced to withdraw elsewhere to save their lives. Mountain doves are contrasted with doves of the valleys, as wild animals are with domestic ones. Thus in Hesychius, Semiramis is περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], as has already been explained. And in the Alcamus العزف [al-ʿazf] Alozpho is الحمام الطورانية [al-ḥamām al-ṭūrāniyya], mountain dove.
